query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying an ultrathin, air‐sprayed 2D transition metal dichalcogenide high‐entropy alloy (HEA) coating to bulk HEA components will induce a tribocatalytic formation of a stable, lubricious glaze during sliding. This self‐organized interface will decrease both the coefficient of friction and the wear rate compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk high‐entropy alloy components (e.g., typical BCC HEAs) with conventional microstructure not possessing a dedicated lubricating phase.
generation.intervention: Air‐spray deposition of a 2D HEA coating based on a composition such as (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 that combines a layered, transition metal dichalcogenide structure with high-entropy design.
generation.conditions: The intervention is expected to be effective over a wide service-temperature range (from room temperature up to approximately 800 °C) and under varied loading conditions encountered in self‐lubricating moving components.
generation.structural_mediator: The nanoscale, layered structure of the 2D HEA coating promotes stress-induced tribocatalytic reactions that generate a continuous, in-situ lubricious glaze layer.
generation.mechanism: Under sliding contact, the 2D coating’s layered nanostructure facilitates the formation of a dense oxide/glaze layer (via tribocatalytic reactions) that serves as a self-lubricating film. This film minimizes adhesive wear and reduces friction by acting as a low-shear interface between contacting surfaces.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated HEA surfaces, coated components should exhibit a substantial reduction in both the friction coefficient (potentially 30–50% lower) and wear rate due to the continuous formation of a protective, lubricious layer during operation.
generation.baseline: Untreated HEA components that do not benefit from the tribocatalytically induced lubricious interface, showing higher friction and increased wear rates under similar service conditions.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the intervention depends on the reliable adhesion of the ultrathin coating to the HEA substrate and its ability to remain intact under repeated thermal cycling and mechanical stresses. Its benefit may be compromised if the coating delaminates or if environmental factors (e.g., excessive oxidation beyond the controlled glaze formation) occur.
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies indicate promising tribological performance in 2D HEA coatings and nanopatterned adaptive interfaces, the precise quantitative improvements in COF and wear rate, as well as the long-term durability of the coating under complex service conditions, remain to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one set coated with the 2D (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 HEA coating via air-spray deposition and one set left uncoated as the control. Perform standardized ball‐on‐disk sliding tests over a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C, under identical loads. Use in-situ sensors and post-test surface analyses (e.g., microscopy, XRD, and EDS) to monitor the formation and integrity of the lubricious glaze layer, as well as to record friction coefficient and wear rate.
measurements: Surface morphology and coating integrity via microscopy
Phase composition of any in-situ formed glaze layer (using XRD/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in both friction coefficient and wear rate compared to the uncoated controls across the tested temperature range, or if no stable lubricious glaze layer forms under sliding, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

To examine the longevity and performance of the HEA coating for extended durations, the long‐run endurance tests were performed till failure at different loads of 1N, 5N, and 9N. Interestingly, the experiments show that 2D HEA lubricant works better at higher loads (Figure 2d). The tests ran for sliding distances of 525, 1040, and 1590 m at 1, 5, and 9N, respectively, before failure. So far, the superior lubricious effect of 2D HEA could be demonstrated from the low friction and wear rates, also accompanied by its extended longevity, especially much better performance at high loads, which increases the interest in the friction mechanism of 2D HEA.

These studies illustrate that preparing high-entropy alloy coatings via laser cladding technology is an effective method to enhance the thermal stability of materials. Further reinforcement and refinement of CCA systems are imperative to ensure their reliable performance under increasingly harsh service environments. In our previous research [], ultrasonic surface-rolling strengthening technology was employed to apply periodic impact forces on the surface of Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 laser-clad coatings, refining surface grains and thereby improving the wear resistance and corrosion resistance of the coatings. However, this equipment is expensive, and processing complex precision-structural components is challenging. In recent years, numerous studies have focused on improving the coarse microstructure in high-entropy alloy systems by adding specific proportions of rare-earth elements, purifying the molten pool, and reducing the dilution rate between the cladding layer and the substrate to achieve higher component performance.
